note: Trimmed export of a real session (ids and user_id removed): Toyota Platz 2001, rear-left wheel bearing, then an intermittent ABS light after a hub swap. Message 3 is the synthetic 'Please continue' user turn the old client stored.

state.title: Bumpy-road ABS light after new hub
safety_flags: When the ABS light is on, anti-lock braking is disabled but conventional brakes still work — drive as if you have no ABS: longer gaps, gentler braking in the wet, and extra care on slippery or gravelly roads.

A bump-triggered flickering ABS light is a real intermittent sensor-circuit fault, not cosmetic; it means ABS may not operate in a panic stop. Sort the connector/harness before relying on ABS in wet conditions.
The ABS sensor was disconnected during diagnosis — reconnect it fully until it clicks, and confirm the ABS warning light comes on at key-on and goes out after a few seconds.
Do not reuse the old hub nut — it is normally a one-use staked/crushed nut; fit a new one to the Toyota-specified torque rather than guessing.
Verify the new hub nut was replaced and torqued to Toyota spec; an under-torqued hub can shift and cause ABS faults or wheel damage.
If the new hub shows play, makes noise, or its torque is unknown, do not drive until it is checked.
If the back of the car ever feels vague or steps sideways, stop and get it recovered rather than driven.
When jacking, use flat solid ground, chock the front wheels, and support the rear on jack stands; never work under a car held only by a jack.
Keep hands clear of spinning hub/wheel parts during testing.

suspected_causes.cause: ABS sensor connector half-latched or terminal disturbed
suspected_causes.evidence: The ABS light began after the sensor was disconnected during hub work and now flickers on bumpy roads. A bump-triggered intermittent light fits a connector that is not fully clicked home, a backed-out or bent pin, corrosion, moisture, or a missing seal.
suspected_causes.next_check: Unplug and reseat the ABS sensor connector until it clicks; inspect both halves for corrosion, moisture, a bent/backed-out pin and a missing rubber seal. Then key on and watch the ABS self-test.

suspected_causes.cause: ABS sensor harness strained or chafed near the hub
suspected_causes.evidence: The hub was replaced, which can pull the flexible sensor harness taut, twist it, or leave a clip off so the wire rubs. A strand broken inside intact insulation is intermittent and shows up when suspension moves over bumps.
suspected_causes.next_check: With the car safely on stands, trace the sensor wire from the hub along the axle/trailing arm. Look for a stretched run, missing/popped clip, shiny rub mark or kink. Gently flex the harness while someone watches the ABS light at key-on.

suspected_causes.cause: New hub tone ring or sensor seating/air gap
suspected_causes.evidence: A new complete hub brings a new tone ring and changes the sensor's air gap. If the sensor is not fully seated, its mount is loose, or the new ring has paint, rust, grit, a damaged tooth or runout, the signal can drop out over bumps.
suspected_causes.next_check: Pull the sensor, inspect its tip and the tone ring, spin the hub and watch the ring for runout or a cracked/missing tooth, wipe it clean, press the sensor fully into its bore and torque its bolt. Get any air-gap/resistance spec from a Toyota source rather than guessing.

suspected_causes.cause: New hub nut not renewed or not torqued to spec / hub not fully seated
suspected_causes.evidence: A new hub is fitted, but if the hub nut was reused or under-torqued, the hub can shift and change the ABS sensor air gap, and this can appear as a bump-triggered intermittent light. It is also a wheel-security concern.
suspected_causes.next_check: Confirm a new one-use hub nut was fitted and torqued to the Toyota-specified figure. Rock the hub at 12–6 and 3–9 o'clock and compare with the right rear; if there is play or torque is unknown, have it checked before driving further.

messages.content:
when I am driving I hear a rhythmic ga ga noise from the back of my car. around 20 to 35 km/h then the rhythm goes fast and goes quiet

When it happens: Accelerating

**Before you dig in:** a rhythmic noise from the back of the car is usually wheel-end, but it's worth a two-minute safety check first — with the car parked, put a wrench on each rear wheel nut and make sure none are loose, and look at the rear tires for bubbles or bulges in the sidewall. A loose wheel or a failing tire can produce exactly this kind of noise and is dangerous. If you ever feel it through the seat as a shake or the car feels vague, stop driving.

Nothing in your description suggests an engine or transmission fault — a rhythmic noise tied to road speed, coming from one end of the car, points at things that rotate with the wheels.

**Most likely causes, in order**

1. **Rear tire damage or irregular wear** — this best explains the *rhythmic* character: a cupped/scalloped tread, a flat-spotted tire, a slipped belt, or a stone/nail/wheel weight stuck or missing gives one "ga" per wheel revolution, so the rhythm speeds up exactly with road speed. At 20–35 km/h the repetition is slow enough to hear as separate beats; above that it blurs into a hum and gets masked by road noise, which matches it "going quiet."
   *Check:* engine off, car parked. Run your palm slowly around each rear tire's tread — feel for sawtooth scalloping, a raised/lowered spot, or anything embedded. Look for a bulge in the sidewall. Compare left and right, and spin the wheel by hand to watch that the tread runs true (no side-to-side wobble = no bent rim).

2. **Rear wheel bearing** — this explains the *accelerating* part best: bearing noise changes with load, so it can be louder under power and quieter when you lift off or coast. It's less likely than a tire to sound like distinct "ga ga" beats, though a damaged ball or race does produce one knock per revolution. No passage here covers the Platz's rear bearings specifically, so this is general guidance: worn bearings typically make a whirring or rumbling noise (Automotive Engine Repair, p. 198 — that passage is about engine accessory bearings, but the principle is the same).
   *Check:* jack the rear of the car on flat, solid ground, chock the front wheels, and support it on stands. Grab each rear tire at 12 and 6 o'clock and rock it, then at 3 and 9 o'clock. Any rock or clunk, or a gritty/rough feel when you spin the wheel, points to the bearing. Compare sides — usually only one is bad.

3. **Rear brake drag** — less likely to be rhythmic, but a sticking rear brake or a drum with a warped surface can rub once per revolution and will be worse under load. The Platz manual's warning-noise note describes brake pad wear indicators as a *squeal or scrape* when pads are worn, and warns that rotor damage follows if you ignore it (Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 141) — your "ga ga" doesn't really match that sound, which is why this ranks third.
   *Check:* after a normal drive, carefully compare the temperature of the two rear wheels (they'll be hot — use a quick light touch or an IR thermometer). One noticeably hotter wheel means that brake is dragging. Also note whether a light brake application changes the noise.

**Three quick tests that separate these**
- **Coast in neutral at ~30 km/h** (safe, straight road). If the noise is unchanged, it's wheel-end (tire or bearing), not the drivetrain. If it disappears, come back to me — that changes the picture.
- **Gentle S-turns at ~30 km/h.** A bearing usually gets louder or quieter when you load one side; a bad tire usually doesn't change much.
- **Light braking.** If it stops or changes pitch only when braking, suspect the brake.

Engine noises can be pinpointed with a stethoscope or a length of hose held against the suspect part (Automotive Engines Diagnosis Repair Rebuilding, p. 97), but for a wheel-end noise, spinning the wheel by hand with the car safely raised is more useful.

I couldn't find the Platz's rear wheel nut torque or rear bearing specs in these references, so have the nuts checked to spec rather than guessing a number.

Two questions so I can narrow it down:
1. Does the noise change when you turn left versus right at that speed?
2. With the car safely jacked up and the rear wheels off the ground, does either rear wheel feel rough or have play when you rock it?
I checked both left and right rear tires they are good. lifted both sides and spun the they don't wobble but the rear left tire has the same ga ga noise I was hearing only smaller
Please continue from my last saved message. Do not repeat it.

Good — that's a genuinely useful result. Reproducing the noise with the rear left wheel off the ground and no load on it means this is **not** load-dependent. That weakens the "bearing noise only under acceleration" theory and strengthens something that makes one beat per wheel revolution regardless of load. It also confirms the problem is at the rear left corner, which rules out the diff, driveshaft and transmission.

Caveat on citations: the Platz manual excerpts I have here are all audio-system pages (CD/radio functions), so I have no Platz-specific spec for the rear hub, bearing or drum. Everything below is general guidance.

**Revised ranking**

1. **Rear left tire — still the best fit (raised confidence).** "The tires look good" only rules out the obvious — a cupped/scalloped tread, a flat spot from a hard stop, a slipped belt, or a nail head/stone/screw flush with the tread still make one "ga" per revolution and are easy to miss by eye. The noise surviving with no load on the wheel fits this perfectly.
   *Next check:* spin the wheel slowly and watch one full revolution of the tread closely for a high or low spot, an embedded object, or a clean rectangular patch on the rim where a wheel weight has fallen off. Then run your palm around the tread in one direction, then the other — cupping feels like sawteeth, smooth one way and rough the other.

2. **Rear left wheel bearing — now second, but not eliminated.** A bearing with one damaged ball or a dry race can click or thump once per revolution even spun by hand, though it usually adds a grit or rumble you can feel. The definitive split is the wheel-off test in a moment.
   *Next check:* with the wheel off, spin the bare hub and listen and feel. Also rock the hub at 12–6 and 3–9 o'clock — any play or grit means bearing.

3. **Rear left brake drag or drum contact — worth checking while you're there.** A warped drum, a rust ridge on the drum edge, a shoe that's shifted, or a bent backing plate dust shield touching the drum will rub once per revolution and can sound like a slow "ga-ga." It wouldn't necessarily be worse under power, which matches today's finding.
   *Next check:* look for a shiny scuff ring or bare-metal rub mark on the drum edge or backing plate, and check for dark grease/oil inside the drum area (a leaking axle seal contaminates the shoes).

**The test that settles it: spin the hub with the wheel off**

Car on stands on flat solid ground, chocks at the front, in Park with the parking brake off for the left rear. Take the left rear wheel off and spin the bare hub by hand.
- Noise **gone** → it's the tire. Get that tire inspected off the rim by a shop, or swap the rear wheels left-to-right and see if the noise moves to the right side.
- Noise **still there** → it's the bearing, drum, or brake, and the tire is innocent.

Don't put your hands or fingers into the wheel arch while anything is spinning, and never work under a car held only by a jack.

Two questions:
1. When you spun the left rear, was the sound a soft thump/beat, or more of a gritty scrape or rumble?
2. Roughly how many "ga"s per second at that speed — and did it stay the same when you spun it faster?
tire off and only spinning only the hub the sound is still there, the sound is once per revolution

That result changes the picture cleanly: **the tire is out of the running.** A noise that's still there with the wheel off, once per revolution, and with no load on it is coming from the hub assembly itself — the bearing or the brake/drum inboard of it. Still rear left only, so your current causes 1 and 2 (tire) can be dropped and cause 2 (bearing) and 3 (brake) are now what's left.

**Revised ranking**

1. **Rear left wheel bearing / hub bearing — now the leading cause.** One beat per revolution with no load, no wheel wobble, and the tire eliminated is the classic signature of a single damaged ball or spalled race: one rough spot makes one click or thump each time it passes the load zone. General principle, and it fits your findings: worn bearings are a standard cause of a whirring or rumbling noise (Automotive Engine Repair, p. 215), and the same passage notes that a noise still present with the drivetrain unloaded points at the wheels, tires or axles rather than the engine or gearbox (Automotive Engine Repair, p. 215) — which is exactly what your hand-spin reproduced.
   *Next check:* spin the bare hub slowly and listen at the hub itself, and feel for a single rough spot or a slight catch as it comes round each revolution. Rock the hub at 12–6 and 3–9 o'clock and compare with the right rear. Grit felt through your fingertips, or a click you can feel as well as hear, confirms the bearing.

2. **Rear left brake — drum, shoe or dust shield contact (still live).** A warped drum, a rust ridge at the drum edge catching a shoe, a shoe that's shifted, or a bent backing plate/dust shield rubbing the drum all give one rub per revolution and wouldn't be load-dependent, so this matches today's result just as well as the bearing does. It stays second only because a rub usually sounds like a scrape rather than a distinct "ga."
   *Next check:* the drum-off spin below, plus look for a shiny scuff ring or bare-metal rub mark on the drum edge or dust shield, and for dark grease inside the drum area that would mean a leaking axle seal has contaminated the shoes.

3. **Loose or damaged hub nut / stub axle flange — worth ruling out while it's apart.** A hub nut that has worked loose lets the hub shift slightly and can make a once-per-revolution knock. I couldn't find the Platz's rear hub nut torque or rear bearing specification in these references, so don't guess a torque — have it checked to spec.

**The decisive test: spin it again with the drum off**

Car on stands, front chocked, parking brake off, transmission in Park. Take the drum off the left rear and spin the bare hub flange again.
- Noise **gone** → it's the drum, shoes or dust shield. This is the cheaper and more common outcome, and you may be able to fix it yourself.
- Noise **still there** → the bearing is confirmed. On this era of small Toyota, the rear bearing is usually pressed into the drum hub and needs a press or a proper puller to swap, plus a new hub nut — that's a job for a shop, or at minimum an experienced DIYer with the right tools.

One caveat on today's test: on many rear-drum cars the drum is only held by the wheel nuts, so with the wheel off the drum can sit slightly loose and rattle on its own. If the "ga" you heard was fainter and more rattly than what you hear driving, it may have been the loose drum rather than the bearing. The drum-off spin above resolves that.

One more reason not to leave it: a rear bearing that's starting to fail can develop play or seize, and a rear wheel that lets go at speed is a serious hazard. Until it's fixed, keep speeds low, avoid sustained highway driving, and if you ever feel the back of the car vague or step sideways, stop and get it recovered rather than driven.

Two questions:
1. When you spun the hub, was the drum still on, or did you have it off?
2. Is the sound a crisp metallic click/tick — or more of a dry scrape or rub? That alone pushes it toward bearing or brake.
okay took off the wheel hub from the brake drum and disconnected the ABS sensor connector, the issue was the bearing

Confirmed, then — **rear left wheel bearing.** That also closes out the brake option: with the hub off the drum and the noise still present, the drum, shoes and dust shield are innocent. Drop the brake and hub-nut causes from your list; this is bearing only.

Two things to handle before it goes back together:

**The ABS sensor you unplugged.** With the sensor disconnected the ABS warning light will come on and the anti-lock system will not operate — but the brakes still work conventionally (<Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 140>). Reconnect it fully and push the connector home until it clicks. Then check the light: at key-on it should come on and go out after a few seconds if the system is healthy — the same page describes that self-test behaviour (<Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 140>). If it stays lit after reassembly, the sensor or its air gap/ring got disturbed during the hub removal, and that needs sorting before you rely on ABS in the wet.

**The hub nut.** These are normally a one-use staked or crushed nut — do not reuse the old one, and don't guess a torque. I couldn't find the Platz's rear hub nut torque or rear bearing spec in these references, so get the figure from a Toyota source or have the shop set it.

**What the job involves.** On this car the rear bearing is pressed into the hub/drum assembly, so it needs a hydraulic press or proper bearing puller and driver set — that's the point where it's genuinely a shop job (or an experienced DIYer with a press). If you're handing it over, tell them: rear left bearing confirmed by hand-spin with the wheel and drum off, ABS sensor disconnected during diagnosis and needs reconnecting.

**While it's apart, worth a look:** the wheel cylinder for brake fluid weeping, the shoes for contamination, and the drum inner face for a rust ridge. Cheap to check now, annoying to revisit.

**Until it's fixed:** keep speeds low, avoid sustained highway driving, and if the back end ever feels vague or steps sideways, stop and get recovered rather than driven — a bearing that's already noisy unloaded can develop play or seize.

Nice piece of diagnosis, by the way — the wheel-off, then drum-off spin is exactly what separated the three candidates.
so I have been driving it and the ABS light comes on and disappears

The intermittent light is the sensor circuit talking, and the timing points straight at your diagnostic work: an ABS light that flickers on and off after the sensor was unplugged and the hub was off is usually a connector or air-gap problem, not a new fault.

**One reassurance first.** When the ABS light is on and the brake warning light is off, the anti-lock function is disabled but the brakes still work conventionally (<Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 140>). So you're not brakeless — but you have no ABS in that moment, which matters most on wet or slippery roads (<Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 141>). Don't treat a flickering light as cosmetic; in a panic stop on a wet road it's the difference the system was fitted for.

**Why it comes and goes.** A fault that's present at key-on keeps the light lit; once the fault stops being detected, the light extinguishes and the system self-tests again at the next key cycle — the light comes on with the key and goes out after a few seconds if all is well (<Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 140>). The manual also notes that if a light that came on while driving goes out and doesn't return, that's normal operation (<Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 141>). What separates "normal" from "a real problem" for you is **repetition** — a one-off after the reconnect is expected, a light that keeps flickering is a genuine intermittent signal.

**Most likely causes, in order**

1. **Sensor connector not fully latched, or a terminal disturbed.** Best fit: it started right after you disconnected it. The connector must click home; a half-seated plug, a bent or backed-out pin, or green corrosion in the terminals gives a signal that drops in and out over bumps and turns — exactly a flickering light.
   *Check:* unplug and reseat it until it clicks, look into both halves with a light for corrosion, moisture or a pushed-back pin, and check the rubber seal is present. Then key on and watch the self-test.

2. **Sensor wiring strained at the hub end.** The flexible section between the body and the hub takes the suspension movement, and removing the hub often pulls it taut or twists it. A wire broken inside intact insulation is intermittent by nature.
   *Check:* with the car safely on stands, have someone turn the steering / bounce that corner gently while you watch and gently flex the harness section near the hub. Look for a stretched or kinked run, or a clip that's come off and let the wire rub.

3. **Sensor not fully seated, or tone ring/debris disturbed.** The sensor reads the ring on the hub; if the sensor sits slightly proud, or rust, grit or a bit of the old bearing debris got onto the ring, the signal drops out at certain speeds.
   *Check:* pull the sensor, wipe the tip and the ring, look for a crack or missing tooth on the ring, and press the sensor fully into its bore.

4. **Hub bearing play (only if the bearing hasn't been replaced).** A hub with play changes the sensor air gap as it moves, which produces an intermittent signal that can look exactly like this. If the old bearing is still in there, sorting it may fix the light too.
   *Check:* rock the hub at 12–6 and 3–9 o'clock and compare with the right rear.

I have no resistance or air-gap specification for this sensor in these references, so don't chase a number from me — if it comes to measuring, get the figure from a Toyota source.

**Until it's sorted:** drive as if you have no ABS — longer gaps, gentler braking in the wet, and treat a wet or gravelly road with extra care, since anti-lock is designed to help with lock-up on slippery surfaces (<Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 141>).

Two questions so I can pin it down:
1. Has the bearing actually been replaced and the new hub nut fitted, or is the old bearing still in the car?
2. Does the light come on at a particular moment — over bumps, in turns, at a certain speed, or randomly?

Bumpy-road-only is the most useful clue yet — it points hard at a **loose connection or a wire flexing**, not at the sensor's internals. A bump throws the suspension through its travel, which tugs the sensor harness and shifts the connector; the signal drops for an instant, the light latches on, then the next key cycle self-tests clean and it goes out again. That's exactly the "comes on while driving, then doesn't return" pattern the manual describes, with the light going out after a few seconds at key-on if the system is healthy (<Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 140>).

One thing not to misread: that same page notes a light that came on and then went out and stayed out is normal operation (<Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 140>). Yours is repeating on bumps, so it's a real intermittent fault, not the normal case. And while the light is on, anti-lock is disabled but the brakes still work conventionally (<Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 140>) — so keep driving gently in the wet until it's fixed.

**Revised ranking**

1. **Sensor connector half-latched or a terminal disturbed (raised to top).** Best fit: it began right after you unplugged it, and it's now bump-triggered. A plug that's clicked but not fully home, a backed-out pin, or corrosion in the terminals breaks contact on impacts.
   *Check:* unplug, look into both halves with a light for a pushed-back or bent pin, green corrosion or moisture, and confirm the rubber seal is there. Push it home until it clicks, then do the wiggle test below.

2. **Harness strained or chafed near the hub.** Second best fit for a bump-specific fault. Removing the hub often pulls the flexible section taut, twists it, or leaves a clip off so the wire rubs. A strand broken inside intact insulation is intermittent by nature and shows up on bumps, not on smooth road.
   *Check:* on stands, follow the wire from the sensor back along the axle/trailing arm. Look for a stretched run, a missing or popped clip, a shiny rub mark, or a kink. Then gently flex the harness section by hand while someone watches the light at key-on — if you can make the light come on by flexing, you've found it.

3. **Sensor not fully seated, or its mount loose.** If the sensor sits slightly proud or its bolt is loose, bumps change the air gap and the signal drops out. Also check the tone ring for rust, grit or a cracked/missing tooth.
   *Check:* pull the sensor, wipe the tip and the ring, press it fully into its bore and torque the bolt properly. I have no air-gap or resistance figure for this sensor in these references — don't guess one; get it from a Toyota source if you need to measure.

4. **Hub bearing play (only if the old bearing is still fitted).** Still worth confirming, because play in the hub moves the tone ring relative to the sensor and mimics a wiring fault — and a bump is when that play shows up.
   *Check:* rock the hub at 12–6 and 3–9 o'clock and compare with the right rear.

**The test that finds it:** car on stands on flat solid ground, front chocked, key ON so the ABS light is in its self-test state, then have someone gently bounce and rock that corner — or push the trailing arm up and down a little — while you watch the light and flex the harness by hand. Bumps are the trigger you're trying to reproduce, so do it with the suspension moving, not just by wiggling the plug.

Two questions:
1. Has the bearing actually been replaced yet, or is the old one still in the car?
2. Does the light seem tied to one corner — did it start after you worked on the left rear specifically, or does any bump anywhere set it off?
it is a new wheel hub on the car

That narrows it further: with a new hub and bearing fitted, the "play in the old bearing shifting the air gap" cause is off the table — assuming the new hub is torqued to spec. So the bump-triggered light is now down to the sensor circuit itself, and specifically to something the hub replacement disturbed.

On citations: none of the passages I have this turn cover the Platz's ABS sensor, tone ring or hub, so everything below is general guidance, not a Platz-specific spec.

**Revised ranking**

1. **Connector not fully latched, or a terminal disturbed — still top.** It started after you unplugged the sensor, and bumps are exactly what breaks a half-seated contact. Nothing about a new hub changes this.
   *Check:* unplug, inspect both halves for a backed-out or bent pin, green corrosion, moisture in the boot, and a missing seal. Push it home until it clicks.

2. **Harness strained, kinked or unclipped during the hub swap — second, and slightly higher now.** Fitting a hub means the trailing arm and hub move around; the flexible section can end up pulled taut, twisted, or left out of its clip so it rubs. A strand broken inside intact insulation only shows up when the suspension moves.
   *Check:* with the car on stands, trace the wire from the sensor back along the arm — stretched run, popped clip, shiny rub mark, or a sharp bend. Flex it gently by hand while someone watches the light at key-on.

3. **Sensor not seated against the new hub, or the new hub's tone ring is the problem — raised now.** On a replacement hub the tone ring comes with it, so this is a fresh variable: the sensor may not be pressed fully into its bore against the new hub, the bolt may not be tight, or the ring itself may have shipping paint, rust, grit, a damaged tooth, or (on a cheap hub) be pressed on slightly crooked. Any of those gives a marginal signal that drops out on bumps.
   *Check:* pull the sensor, look at its tip and the ring, spin the hub and watch the ring for runout or a missing/cracked tooth, wipe the ring clean, then seat the sensor fully and tighten its bolt. I have no air-gap or resistance figure for this sensor — get it from a Toyota source rather than guessing.

**Dropped:** hub bearing play. Confirm the new hub nut was fitted new and torqued to the Toyota figure — an under-torqued hub nut can let the hub shift and would bring this back.

**The test that finds it:** car on stands on flat solid ground, front chocked, key ON, then have someone bounce and rock that corner while you watch the light and flex the harness by hand. Reproduce it with the suspension moving, not just by wiggling the plug — bumps are your trigger.

Until it's fixed, drive as if you have no ABS: longer gaps, gentler braking in the wet (<Toyota Platz 2001 manual (s3.amazonaws.com), p. 140> — that page confirms conventional brakes still work with the light on).

Two questions:
1. Was the ABS light completely absent before the hub was replaced — it only started after? That tells me whether this is installation-induced.
2. Did you fit a complete hub assembly (bearing and tone ring together), or have a bearing pressed into the old hub?
